title: “HE MAKES ALL THINGS NEW.”
paragraphs: “HE MAKES ALL THINGS NEW.”

Not patched.
Not upgraded.
Not improved.
New.

The week drained you.
The mistakes replayed.
The guilt whispered, “You’ll never change.”
But the last pages of the Bible thunder something different.
📖 Book of Revelation 21
The apostle John sees the curtain pulled back on eternity. And what he sees is not a repair job.
It’s a wedding.
A city.
A voice from the throne.
“Behold, the dwelling place of God is with man… He will wipe away every tear… death shall be no more…” (Revelation 21:3–4)
Pause there.
Every tear.

Not ignored.
Not minimized.
Wiped.

That means the tears you cried in secret.
The betrayal nobody apologized for.
The addiction you swore you’d quit by Monday.

He sees it.
And He promises an ending to it.
But let’s not sanitize the story.
Revelation comes after judgment. After beasts. After bowls of wrath. Sin is not brushed aside. Evil is not excused.
God doesn’t renew the world by pretending it wasn’t broken.
He deals with sin fully—through the blood of Jesus Christ.
That’s the center.
Because when the voice from the throne declares:
“Behold, I am making all things new.” (Revelation 21:5)
He speaks as the same One who once said from a cross:
“It is finished.”
The new creation is possible because the old sin was paid for.

Some scholars interpret the “new heaven and new earth” as complete cosmic recreation. Others see it as a radical renewal of the present creation. Either way—don’t miss this—the renewal is anchored in Christ’s finished work.

No cross.
No new city.
No wiped tears.
And then John describes the New Jerusalem—radiant like a bride. Gates of pearl. Streets like pure gold. No temple—because the Lord Himself is the temple.
No sun—because His glory lights it.
No night.
No curse.
Do you see the reversal?

Genesis began with a garden and lost communion.
Revelation ends with a city and restored communion.

Sin drove us out.
Grace brings us home.
But here’s the tension.
Revelation 21 also warns:
“But as for the cowardly, the faithless… their portion will be in the lake that burns with fire…” (v.8)
There it is.
Two destinies.
This is not poetic exaggeration. This is holy clarity.
New creation is not automatic. It is received.
And how?

Not by self-improvement.
Not by church attendance alone.
Not by vibes.
By repentance and faith in Jesus Christ.
Verse 6 says, “To the thirsty I will give from the spring of the water of life without payment.”
Thirsty.

Not perfect.
Not polished.
Thirsty.
You feel the dryness? That ache for something clean? That longing to not be defined by your worst moment?
That’s the thirst.
And Christ says: Come.
He makes all things new.

Your past.
Your patterns.
Your identity.
Your future.
Maybe this week exposed your weakness. Good.
Because the New Jerusalem is not for the self-sufficient. It’s for the redeemed.
Lift your head.
The story does not end in ashes. It ends in glory. It ends with God dwelling with His people. It ends with Jesus at the center.
And the invitation is still open.

Repent.
Believe.
Receive the water of life.
He is not finished with you.

He is making.
All things.
New.
“We tell the stories that shame tried to erase.”
